solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Awful, as could be proclamation after gagging order? (11)

annotation.definition2: as could be proclamation after gagging order?

blocks.note: a plain adjective: too dreadful to be put into words

blocks.clueFragment: as could be proclamation after gagging order?
blocks.note: read literally: a proclamation under a gag is not able to be spoken

annotation.surface: A dismal official announcement delivered just after a court has banned any reporting.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half is read literally: UN-SPEAK-ABLE, not able to be spoken. A gagging order is a court ban on publishing something; the question mark flags the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: Something unspeakable is so bad that words fail, hence awful.

entries.clue: One visiting is only misbehaving in raucous manner (7)

indicatorNotes.visiting: a visitor goes inside someone's home, so I goes inside the other letters
indicatorNotes.misbehaving: the letters of IS ONLY behave out of order

blocks.note: IS ONLY rearranged
one = I, the Roman numeral

annotation.surface: A house guest who does nothing but act up and make a racket.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'One visiting' as a rowdy house guest; 'one' is only the Roman numeral, and the guest's visit is the letter going inside.
annotation.definitionFit: Noisily is how something raucous is done.

entries.clue: Fruit that may go off? (9)

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: a real tropical fruit, which can go off by rotting
the reading meant: soldiers' slang for a hand grenade, which goes off by exploding

annotation.surface: A piece of fruit left too long in the bowl, starting to rot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Go off' suggests fruit spoiling, but the joke is the other sense: exploding. Soldiers' slang calls a hand grenade a pineapple for its segmented shape.
annotation.definitionFit: A pineapple is a fruit, and a 'pineapple' grenade is something that goes off.

entries.clue: Gather in a US state (5)

blocks.note: used as printed
Mass. is the short form of Massachusetts

annotation.surface: Crowds assembling somewhere in America.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it places something inside a state, but it only joins definition to wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean collecting things together into a heap.

entries.clue: Intolerance in work unit covered up by colleague (7)

indicatorNotes.covered up by: ALLY wraps round ERG, covering it

blocks.note: an ally is a colleague on your side
the erg is a unit of work in physics

annotation.surface: Office bigotry hushed up by a co-worker.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface paints intolerance as prejudice at work; here it is the body's intolerance of a substance.
annotation.definitionFit: An allergy is the body's intolerance of something such as pollen or nuts.

entries.clue: Lose out, however, in country (7)

indicatorNotes.out: out = wrong, so the letters of LOSE are put out of place

blocks.note: LOSE rearranged
tho' is the informal short form of though, meaning however

annotation.surface: Someone missing out on a chance despite being in the right country.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lose out' reads as a phrasal verb, but it splits: LOSE is the fodder and 'out' the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a small kingdom entirely surrounded by South Africa.

entries.clue: Trip and attempt rugby score? (4,3,4)

blocks.note: to trip up = to make a blunder
a drop goal in rugby starts by dropping the ball onto the foot

annotation.surface: A rugby player stumbles while going for points.
annotation.walkthrough: In rugby a drop goal is scored by dropping the ball and kicking it on the half-volley; the question mark admits the literal reading is a stretch.
annotation.definitionFit: To trip up is to blunder, which is what dropping the ball means figuratively.

entries.clue: Wet water barrier by enclosure (6)

blocks.note: a dam holds back water
a pen is an enclosure for animals

annotation.surface: A soggy barrier standing beside a sheep pen.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wet' reads as an adjective describing the barrier, but it is the verb: to wet something.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: making something moist.

entries.clue: Straighten right angle I bent (7)

indicatorNotes.bent: bent = twisted out of shape, so ANGLE I is twisted

blocks.note: R = right
ANGLE plus I, rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone correcting a right angle they had knocked out of true.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Right angle' reads as one geometric term, but it splits: R, then ANGLE joins I as the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: To realign something is to line it up again, to straighten it.

entries.clue: Titan given time, finally (2,4)

blocks.note: Atlas, the Titan of Greek myth who holds up the sky
T = time

annotation.surface: A giant of myth finally being given some time off.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma makes 'finally' look like an afterthought to the surface; it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: At last means finally, after a long wait.

entries.clue: Heretic converted under the aforementioned Conservative (11)

indicatorNotes.converted: converted = changed, so HERETIC's letters change order
indicatorNotes.under: in a down clue, the rearranged letters sit under THAT

blocks.note: that = the thing just mentioned
HERETIC rearranged

annotation.surface: A heretic who has changed sides and joined the Tory party.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Converted' fits the religious surface of heretic, which disguises it as the anagram signal. A Thatcherite follows Margaret Thatcher, the Conservative British prime minister of 1979 to 1990.
annotation.definitionFit: A Thatcherite is a particular kind of Conservative, a follower of Margaret Thatcher.

entries.clue: Cocktail held back by father – it’s spicy (7)

annotation.definitionNote: a clause describing the answer, which is a noun

indicatorNotes.held: PAPA holds the cocktail inside it
indicatorNotes.back: back = backwards, so KIR turns round

blocks.note: papa = father
kir is a cocktail of white wine and blackcurrant liqueur

annotation.surface: Dad refuses to let someone have a cocktail because it is too fiery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Held back' reads as withheld, but splits into two jobs: 'back' is the turnaround and 'held' the container. 'It's spicy' describes the answer rather than replacing it.
annotation.definitionFit: Paprika is a spice made from dried red peppers.

entries.clue: Erase minor injury (7)

blocks.note: a verb: to strike a name off a list
a noun: a shallow mark on the skin

annotation.walkthrough: Two unrelated senses side by side: a horse withdrawn from a race is struck off the card, and a graze from a cat's claw.
annotation.definitionFit: The verb sense is crossing out or cancelling; the noun sense is a slight graze.

entries.clue: “Hot”, with initial in yellow on tap? (5)

indicatorNotes.initial in: the initial in a word is its first letter

blocks.note: H = hot, as on a tap
and = with
first letter of yellow

annotation.surface: A hot tap marked with a yellow label.
annotation.walkthrough: Hot taps are labelled H, which the surface plays on. 'On tap' means available whenever needed; the question mark nods to the tap pun.
annotation.definitionFit: Something handy is readily available, on tap.

entries.clue: Tiptoe with certain measure past tiger’s relative (9)

indicatorNotes.past: the measure comes past, after, the tiger's relative

blocks.note: a pussy is a cat, a small relative of the tiger
a foot is a fixed measure of length

annotation.surface: Creeping carefully past a tiger's kin.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures someone sneaking past a big cat; in fact the cat is the start of the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean treading softly and stealthily, like a cat.

entries.clue: Stitch cut by knife primarily, little bit wonky (4-5)

indicatorNotes.cut by: SEW is cut open and K put in the gap
indicatorNotes.primarily: primarily = first, so knife gives K

blocks.note: to stitch is to sew
first letter of knife
a whiff is a slight trace

annotation.surface: A seam slashed by a knife ends up a bit crooked.
annotation.walkthrough: Skew-whiff is British informal for crooked or askew.
annotation.definitionFit: Skew-whiff means crooked, not straight: wonky.

entries.clue: Money that is concerning supporter (9)

blocks.note: brass is British slang for money
i.e. = that is
re = concerning

annotation.surface: Financial backing that someone finds worrying.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' suggests a financial backer or a football fan; it is an item of underwear.
annotation.definitionFit: A brassiere is an undergarment that supports the breasts.

entries.clue: Clothes line found after a power cut (7)

indicatorNotes.after: the line and cut come after A and power

blocks.note: used as printed
P = power
to pare is to cut or trim
L = line

annotation.surface: Washing still hanging on the line when the electricity goes off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clothes line' reads as one thing and 'power cut' as another; both pairs split, and 'cut' goes with PARE while 'line' ends the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, somewhat formal: garments collectively, as in the trade term for clothing.

entries.clue: Clever fencing off recreation area – brilliant! (7)

indicatorNotes.fencing off: SLY fences off PARK by surrounding it

blocks.note: sly = cunning, clever
a park is a public space for recreation

annotation.surface: Someone praising a smart plan to fence off a playground.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation 'brilliant!' reads as praise for the plan; it is the definition, meaning shining.
annotation.definitionFit: Something sparkly glitters, so it is brilliant in the sense of bright.

entries.clue: End of discussions, don’t say a word! (5)

annotation.definition: End of discussions, don’t say a word!

indicatorNotes.End of: the end of discussions is its last letter

blocks.note: last letter of discussions
hush! = be quiet

annotation.surface: Someone closing a debate by ordering everyone to be quiet.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: read straight, it is someone calling a halt to talk and ordering silence.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight as an order that ends the talking, which is exactly what the command for silence does.

entries.clue: Cleaner has mop working on floor in studio (7)

indicatorNotes.working: working = in operation, so the letters are set moving
indicatorNotes.on floor in: in a down clue the floor of a word is its bottom, last letter

blocks.note: HAS MOP rearranged
last letter of studio, its floor in a down clue

annotation.surface: A cleaner at work mopping the floor of a studio.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Cleaner' a person; it is a cleaning product, and the mop only supplies letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a soapy liquid for washing hair or carpets, so a kind of cleaning product.

entries.clue: Not just a place for entertainment without roof (6)

indicatorNotes.without roof: in a down clue the roof is the top, first letter, which is removed

blocks.note: a travelling show of rides and stalls; its top letter F goes

annotation.surface: An outdoor venue that is more than just somewhere to have fun.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not just' reads as 'not only', leading into the rest of the sentence; it means unjust.
annotation.definitionFit: Unfair means not just, lacking justice.

entries.clue: Soothing thing, party backing male when on edge (3,4)

indicatorNotes.backing: backing = going backwards, so LAB turns round
indicatorNotes.when on: the party and male go on, after, the edge

blocks.note: a lip is an edge, as of a cup
Lab = the Labour Party
M = male

annotation.surface: A calming presence as a political party backs a man who is feeling tense.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On edge' reads as nervous, but it splits: 'on' places the rest after 'edge', which is LIP.
annotation.definitionFit: Lip balm soothes dry or chapped lips.

entries.clue: Feast upon artist (5)

blocks.note: a verb: to chew steadily and heartily
Edvard, the Norwegian painter of The Scream

annotation.surface: A banquet laid on in honour of a painter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Feast upon artist' reads as a feast held on a painter's behalf; 'upon' belongs with 'Feast' as a phrasal verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Chewing heartily is feasting on food; the second sense names a painter by surname.

entries.clue: Rebuke – why? (4,3)

blocks.note: a noun: a telling-off, in a British idiom
a question asking for the purpose

annotation.surface: Someone being told off and asking the reason.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Give someone what for' is a British idiom for a scolding.
annotation.definitionFit: What for is a scolding in 'give someone what for', and 'what for?' asks why.

entries.clue: Buddy, doll in pieces (6)

blocks.note: bro = brother, buddy
Ken is Barbie's boyfriend doll

annotation.surface: A friend's doll has been smashed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Doll in pieces' reads as a smashed toy; the doll is Ken, and 'in pieces' defines the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: shattered, no longer whole.

entries.clue: Stamp particularly rare originally, I make money collecting it (7)

indicatorNotes.originally: originally = at the start, so the first letters of particularly rare

blocks.note: used as printed
to mint is to make coins
first letters of particularly rare

annotation.surface: A stamp collector who profits from rare specimens.
annotation.walkthrough: The philatelic surface makes 'Stamp' a postage stamp; it is the verb or the mark left, and 'it' simply points back to the PR letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To imprint is to stamp a mark onto something.

entries.clue: Muck about and put down tarot card? (4,3,4)

blocks.note: British informal for clowning around
The Fool is a card in the tarot deck

annotation.surface: A fortune teller messing around while laying out the cards.
annotation.walkthrough: Read literally, playing The Fool is laying down that tarot card; the question mark marks the literal reading.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: acting like a jester is mucking about, and the tarot sense is literal.
